titre: The Defenestration of Prague (1618) and the War It Set Off
accroche: On May 23, 1618, Bohemian nobles throw two regents out of a Prague window, 21 meters up, and set off the Thirty Years' War.
contenu_vulgarise:
On May 23, 1618, in the council chamber of Hradčany Castle in Prague, Protestant nobles of Bohemia put two imperial regents, Vilem Slavata and Jaroslav Martinice, on trial for allowing Protestant chapels to be closed at Broumov and Hrob, in direct violation of the Letter of Majesty that Emperor Rudolf II had granted in 1609. The verdict comes at once, with no possibility of appeal: the two men, then their secretary Philip Fabricius, are seized and thrown out of a second-floor window, a fall of about 21 meters.

## A Botched Execution That Sets Europe Ablaze

All three men survive. This is where the accounts sharply diverge: Catholics see divine intervention, some mentioning the help of angels or the Virgin; Protestant pamphlets say instead that the three men landed on a dung heap that supposedly cushioned their fall, a version historians now consider probably invented after the fact, since no contemporary witness of the scene mentions it. What is certain, on the other hand, is the political aftermath: the defenestration sets off the revolt of the Bohemian Estates against Emperor Ferdinand II. In November 1619, the insurgents offer the crown of Bohemia to a Protestant prince, Frederick V of the Palatinate, crowned on November 4: a year, almost to the day, before imperial troops crush his army at the Battle of White Mountain, on November 8, 1620, at the gates of Prague. By then, the regional revolt, born of a window, has already turned into open war. That war, later known as the Thirty Years' War, would not end until 1648, after ravaging central Europe and costing, by some estimates, several million lives.

## A Window, Not a Cause

This act invented nothing: tensions between Catholics and Protestants in the Habsburg Empire had been simmering for decades, and Bohemia was only one of the religious and political hotspots of an already fractured Europe. But the defenestration supplied what this latent conflict lacked: a precise, dated, symbolic event, capable of tipping a diffuse tension into open revolt and then declared war. It is, moreover, the third time that the people of Prague chose to throw their adversaries out a window rather than confront them any other way: the first defenestration, in 1419, had already preceded the Hussite Wars. The same gesture, almost two centuries apart, and each time the same function: to turn an institutional disagreement into a visible break that no one can any longer ignore or defuse through negotiation.

repere.texte: The three men fall from a height of about 21 meters and all survive: Catholics saw divine intervention, Protestants a dung heap unknown to the witnesses of the time and appearing only after the fact in pamphlets.

carte.punch: Three men thrown from a window 21 meters up set off a thirty-year war.
carte.idee: On May 23, 1618, Protestant nobles of Bohemia throw two imperial regents and their secretary out of a window of Prague Castle, 21 meters up. All three survive, but the act sets off the Bohemian Revolt, then the Thirty Years' War, which ravages Europe until 1648.

quiz.question: Why do the three men thrown out of the window of Prague Castle in 1618 survive a fall of 21 meters?
choix: Because a water-filled moat ran along the castle's facade
Because the window was actually only 3 meters from the ground
The accounts differ: divine intervention for some, a dung heap for others
Because bodyguards had caught them as they fell below
quiz.explication: No contemporary account agrees: Catholics spoke of divine intervention, Protestants of a dung heap, a story that appeared after the fact and was unknown to witnesses of the time, a sign of a propaganda battle more than an established fact.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who are the three men thrown out of the window of Prague Castle on May 23, 1618?
choix: Vilem Slavata, Jaroslav Martinice, and their secretary Philip Fabricius
Emperor Rudolf II and his two military advisers
Three Catholic nobles who came from Vienna to negotiate peace
The governor of Bohemia and his two bodyguards
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text names the two imperial regents Vilem Slavata and Jaroslav Martinice, as well as their secretary Philip Fabricius, tried and then thrown out of the window together.

quiz_supplementaire.question: For what reason do the Protestant nobles of Bohemia put the two imperial regents on trial before throwing them out of the window?
choix: They refused to pay an extraordinary tax voted by the emperor
They had allowed Protestant chapels to be closed, against the Letter of Majesty of 1609
They had had several Protestant nobles arrested without trial
They had tried to impose a new Catholic bishop on Prague
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The regents had allowed Protestant chapels to be closed at Broumov and Hrob, in direct violation of the Letter of Majesty granted by Rudolf II in 1609.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happens on November 8, 1620, nearly a year after Frederick V of the Palatinate was crowned king of Bohemia?
choix: Frederick V signs a peace treaty with Emperor Ferdinand II
The Letter of Majesty of 1609 is officially repealed
Imperial troops crush his army at the Battle of White Mountain
The Bohemian Estates elect a second Protestant king
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text places the Battle of White Mountain on November 8, 1620, almost a year after Frederick V's coronation on November 4, 1619, and describes the crushing of his army at the gates of Prague.
